variants.name: std::thread::scope workers + mpsc job queue (Rust 1.63+)
variants.implementation_notes: Rust's literal realization is std::thread::scope plus channels: scope guarantees every spawned thread is joined before the scope returns and lets workers borrow the master's non-'static data (input slices) without Arc, sync_channel(bound) is the work queue and gives backpressure, and dropping the sender after the last job makes the workers' recv loop end (a disconnect is a normal result, not an error). Each ScopedJoinHandle::join returns the worker's partial result ready for a deterministic combine, and a panic inside a worker is re-raised by join (or by scope), so failure handling is explicit. Std has no pool, no queue type and no work stealing; share the Receiver through a Mutex, or move to rayon/tokio when the workload justifies a real scheduler.
pitfalls: std's Receiver is not Sync: share it as Mutex<Receiver> (serialising only the pop) or give each worker its own channel; a naive Arc<Receiver> does not compile.
join().unwrap() turns a panicking worker into a master panic, and dropping unjoined handles abandons their results - define whether one failed worker fails the batch.
Any live sender (for example one cloned into a worker) keeps recv() from returning None, so the worker loop never ends.
Scoped borrows forbid the master mutating shared data while workers run: all combination happens after the scope, which is also the synchronisation point.

variants.name: Rayon work-stealing pool with par_iter / scope
variants.implementation_notes: Rayon is the dominant library realization: par_iter converts a sequential iterator into a parallel one, the global work-stealing pool schedules the split work across the cores, and the reduce/collect that ends the chain is the master's combine - the coordinator role disappears into the runtime. rayon::scope is the escape hatch when the number of tasks is dynamic or tasks must borrow local data, and ThreadPoolBuilder builds a private pool when the master needs isolation from other rayon users. Use it when sub-tasks are uniform, independent and expressed naturally as an iteration; the central work queue, admission control and heterogeneous job types of the classic master are not part of this variant.
pitfalls: The global pool is shared process-wide: blocking or sleeping inside a parallel closure starves every other rayon user.
Side effects inside par_iter closures run in unspecified order and across threads; keep the closures pure and the reduce operation associative.
Nested parallelism is managed by rayon - do not spawn ad hoc threads or private pools per call, which oversubscribes and loses work stealing.
For heterogeneous jobs, an explicit queue and rayon::scope (or crossbeam channels) is a better fit than par_iter over an index range.

variants.name: Tokio JoinSet fan-out for I/O-bound sub-tasks
variants.implementation_notes: JoinSet<T> is a collection of tasks spawned on the Tokio runtime and is itself the join handle set: join_next().await yields results in completion order (aggregate as they arrive), join_all consumes the set, and dropping the set aborts every task - Tokio's cancellation discipline, which is exactly the master's shutdown lever. Use it when sub-tasks are I/O-bound and each awaits sockets or files; CPU-bound sub-tasks must go through spawn_blocking or leave the runtime entirely, because they block a worker thread. All tasks in one set share the result type, so heterogeneous partials need an enum wrapper.
pitfalls: Dropping the JoinSet aborts every running task silently - keep it alive until the aggregate is complete, or results vanish.
CPU-bound code on the async runtime blocks a worker thread; use spawn_blocking or a dedicated thread pool.
A panicking task surfaces as a JoinError from join_next, so panic policy (resume vs fail the batch) is an explicit master decision.
All tasks in a set share one result type: wrap heterogeneous partials in an enum or use separate sets.
